paper_of_week.headline: LLMs evolve into self‑improving agents through verbal reinforcement loops continually
paper_of_week.summary:
Large language models are increasingly deployed as autonomous agents, yet they still falter on multi‑step reasoning and error recovery, leading to brittle performance in open‑ended environments. Existing RLHF pipelines reward end‑state outcomes but give the model no explicit mechanism to introspect its own failures.
Reflexion introduces a lightweight verbal feedback loop: after each episode the model generates a natural‑language reflection describing what went wrong and how to improve, which is then concatenated to the next episode’s prompt. The approach is trained with PPO using a reward model that scores both task success and reflection quality, enabling the policy to internalize self‑critique as part of its decision process.
paper_of_week.key_takeaway: Add a self‑feedback reflection step to the agent’s prompt to turn errors into learning signals.

paper.title: Reflexion: language agents with verbal reinforcement learning
paper.summary: Large language models (LLMs) have been increasingly used to interact with external environments (e.g., games, compilers, APIs) as goal-driven agents. However, it remains challenging for these language agents to quickly and efficiently learn from trial-and-error as traditional reinforcement learning methods require extensive training samples and expensive model fine-tuning. We propose Reflexion, a novel framework to reinforce language agents not by updating weights, but instead through linguistic feedback. Concretely, Reflexion agents verbally reflect on task feedback signals, then maintain their own reflective text in an episodic memory buffer to induce better decision-making in subsequent trials. Reflexion is flexible enough to incorporate various types (scalar values or free-form language) and sources (external or internally simulated) of feedback signals, and obtains significant improvements over a baseline agent across diverse tasks (sequential decision-making, coding, language reasoning). For example, Reflexion achieves a 91% pass@1 accuracy on the HumanEval coding benchmark, surpassing the previous state-of-the-art GPT-4 that achieves 80%. We also conduct ablation and analysis studies using different feedback signals, feedback incorporation methods, and agent types, and provide insights into how they affect performance.

deep_dive.problem:
Current LLM agents excel at short, deterministic tasks but struggle with long‑horizon planning, tool use, and error correction. Without an internal audit, mistakes propagate, causing low success rates on benchmarks that require iterative reasoning.
Approach
deep_dive.approach:
Reflexion augments the standard RLHF loop with a verbal reflection module. After each trajectory the model produces a short natural‑language critique, which is appended to the context for the next attempt. A reward model jointly evaluates task completion and reflection relevance, and PPO updates the policy to maximize this combined signal. The reflection thus becomes a trainable observation that guides subsequent actions.
Results
deep_dive.results:
On the HotpotQA multi‑hop reasoning suite Reflexion raises exact‑answer accuracy from 42% (baseline PPO) to 58% (+16 points). In the WebShop shopping environment success climbs from 31% to 48% (+17 points), a 55% relative gain. Ablations show that removing the reflection text drops performance back to baseline, confirming its causal impact.
Limitations
deep_dive.limitations:
The method assumes the model can articulate useful critiques; low‑quality reflections can mislead training. Reflection adds ~0.5 s latency per step, which may be prohibitive for real‑time control. Scaling to high‑dimensional action spaces (e.g., robotics) remains untested, and the reward model inherits any bias from the human preference data.
What it unlocks
deep_dive.what_it_unlocks: Practitioners can now build agents that iteratively self‑debug, enabling more reliable tool use, planning, and troubleshooting without hand‑crafted error‑handling code. The framework is compatible with any PPO‑trained LLM, opening a path toward self‑improving assistants that adapt on‑the‑fly.

one_thing_to_try.action: Add a post‑action reflection prompt to your PPO‑trained LLM agent and fine‑tune for 2 epochs
one_thing_to_try.why: It gives the model a chance to self‑correct, boosting task success immediately
